decision.explanation: Separating variables gives y^{1/2} dy=x^{-1/2} dx. Integrating yields (2/3)y^{3/2}=2x^{1/2}+C, so y^{3/2}=3x^{1/2}+K and y=(3x^{1/2}+K)^{2/3}, on intervals where x>0 and 3x^{1/2}+K>0.

after.name: Question 1
after.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}=2{x}^{1/2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C \\ {y}^{3/2} & =3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2})}^{2/3} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+K)}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\frac{3C}{2}.$

content.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=1.$
content.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\sqrt{xy}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{x}\sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =1 \\ \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \sqrt{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \sqrt{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{x}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int {y}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y & =\int {x}^{-1/2}\,\text{d}x \\ \frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2}=2{x}^{1/2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3/2} & =2{x}^{1/2}+C \\ {y}^{3/2} & =3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+\frac{3C}{2})}^{2/3} \\ y & ={(3{x}^{1/2}+K)}^{2/3}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K=\frac{3C}{2}.$

after.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${x}^{2}\,{y}^{′}-y=3$ for $y\ne -3.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\,{y}^{′}-y & =3 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}-y & =3 \\ {x}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y+3 \\ \frac{1}{y+3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y+3}\cdot \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y+3}\,\text{d}y & =\int \frac{1}{{x}^{2}}\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y+3| & =-\frac{1}{x}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y+3|=-\frac{1}{x}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{ln}⁡|y+3| & =-\frac{1}{x}+C \\ |y+3| & ={e}^{-1/x+C} \\ |y+3| & ={e}^{-1/x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y+3| & =K{e}^{-1/x}\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}|y+3| & =K{e}^{-1/x} \\ y+3 & =K{e}^{-1/x} \\ y & =K{e}^{-1/x}-3.\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 4
after.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}=\frac{2x}{3{y}^{2}}.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{2x}{3{y}^{2}} \\ 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =2x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ \int 3{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y & =\int 2x\,\text{d}x \\ {y}^{3} & ={x}^{2}+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
{y}^{3}={x}^{2}+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
y=\sqrt[3]{{x}^{2}+C}.
$$

after.name: Question 5
after.problem: Find the general solution to the differential equation ${y}^{′}=y\operatorname{cos}⁡x$ for $y\ne 0.$
after.worked_solution:
To find the general solution, we first separate the variables:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =y\operatorname{cos}⁡x \\ \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\operatorname{cos}⁡x\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we integrate both sides with respect to $x:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}\,\text{d}x & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\frac{\text{d}y}{\cancel{\text{d}x}}\,\cancel{\text{d}x} & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \int \frac{1}{y}\,\text{d}y & =\int \operatorname{cos}⁡x\,\text{d}x \\ \operatorname{ln}⁡|y| & =\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to the differential equation (in implicit form) is

$$
\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|=\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C.
$$

We're required to write the solution in the form $y=y(x).$ By doing this, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡|y|} & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x+C} \\ |y| & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\cdot {e}^{C} \\ |y| & =K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x},\end{aligned}
$$

where $K={e}^{C}$ and $K>0.$

We can drop the absolute value bars by allowing $K$ to be either positive or negative. Therefore, the most general solution is

$$
y=K{e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}.
$$
